waterParameters.name: Salinity
waterParameters.explanation: How salty the water is, in parts per thousand (ppt). Fresh water is near 0 and sea water is about 35.

waterParameters.name: pH
waterParameters.explanation: How acidic or alkaline the water is, on a scale of 0 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Big swings stress stock.

waterParameters.name: Ammonia
waterParameters.explanation: A waste that builds up from fish droppings and uneaten feed. Even a little can harm gills.

waterParameters.name: Nitrite
waterParameters.explanation: Forms as ammonia breaks down. It makes it harder for stock to carry oxygen in their blood.

waterParameters.name: Nitrate
waterParameters.explanation: The last and mildest stage of waste breakdown. High levels show waste is piling up over time.

waterParameters.name: Dissolved oxygen
waterParameters.explanation: The oxygen in the water that stock breathe. It drops at night, in hot weather and when feed rots.

waterParameters.name: Water temperature
waterParameters.explanation: How warm the water is. Warm water holds less oxygen and makes stock eat and breathe faster.

waterGuidance.title: Within the suggested range
waterGuidance.message: This reading sits inside the demo range. Keep checking at about the same time of day so changes are easy to spot.

waterGuidance.title: Lower than suggested
waterGuidance.message: This reading is below the demo range. Check it again to confirm, watch how your stock behave, and ask a local fisheries technician if it stays low.

waterGuidance.title: Higher than suggested
waterGuidance.message: This reading is above the demo range. Check it again to confirm, watch how your stock behave, and ask a local fisheries technician if it stays high.

waterGuidance.title: Ammonia is higher than suggested
waterGuidance.message: Feed less until it comes down and remove any uneaten feed. If your stock are gasping or not eating, consider changing part of the water where your setup allows it, then check again tomorrow.

waterGuidance.title: Ammonia is higher than suggested
waterGuidance.message: The water in a cage cannot be changed. Feed less until it comes down, clear anything that blocks water flowing through the net, and check again tomorrow.

waterGuidance.title: Nitrite is higher than suggested
waterGuidance.message: Feed less for a day or two and remove uneaten feed. If your stock look weak, consider changing part of the water where your setup allows it, then check again.

waterGuidance.title: Nitrite is higher than suggested
waterGuidance.message: The water in a cage cannot be changed. Feed less for a day or two, keep the net clean so water flows through, and check again.

waterGuidance.title: Nitrate is building up
waterGuidance.message: Waste is collecting over time. Avoid overfeeding, and where your setup allows it, a partial water change may help over the next few days.

waterGuidance.title: Oxygen is lower than suggested
waterGuidance.message: Stop feeding until it recovers. If you have an aerator, run it now, especially overnight. If stock gasp at the surface, get help from a local fisheries technician.

waterGuidance.title: Oxygen is lower than suggested
waterGuidance.message: Stop feeding until it recovers and clear anything that blocks water flowing through the net. If stock gasp at the surface, get help from a local fisheries technician.

waterGuidance.title: The water is warmer than suggested
waterGuidance.message: Warm water holds less oxygen. Feed smaller amounts in the cooler morning and late afternoon, and keep the water at least 1.0-1.2 m deep where you can.

waterRangeGuidance.message: Check readings at about the same time each day. If one leaves its range, feed less and check again before making big changes.
The water in a cage cannot be changed, so feeding and keeping water flowing through the net are the main ways to act on these readings.

steps.title: Choose a spot
steps.instruction: Place the aerator where the water is deep enough to cover it fully, away from the inlet and from where you feed.

steps.title: Keep the power point dry
steps.instruction: Use an outlet sheltered from rain and above flood level. A safety breaker that cuts the power when current leaks into water (RCD or GFCI) is worth adding if you do not have one.

steps.title: Anchor the unit
steps.instruction: Tie the aerator to a stake or a float line so it cannot drift or pull on its cable.

steps.title: Run it and watch
steps.instruction: Switch it on and check that bubbles rise evenly and the water moves. Watch your stock for a few minutes; calm fish near the surface are a good sign.

cautions: Switch off and unplug the aerator before touching it or reaching into the water.
Keep the cable off paths where people walk and away from anything that could cut it.
Follow the supplier's manual wherever it differs from these steps.

steps.title: Screen the intake
steps.instruction: Fit a mesh screen over the intake so the pump cannot draw in fish or leaves.

steps.title: Set it off the bottom
steps.instruction: Rest the pump on a flat stone or brick so it does not suck up mud from the pond or tank floor.

steps.title: Connect the hose
steps.instruction: Push the hose fully onto the outlet and tighten the clamp before the pump goes into the water.

steps.title: Submerge, then switch on
steps.instruction: Lower the pump until it is fully under water, then plug it into a dry, sheltered outlet and check the flow at the hose end.

cautions: Never run the pump out of water; it can overheat within minutes.
Unplug the pump before lifting it out or clearing the intake.
Move only part of the water at a time, as your culture system allows.

steps.title: Cut to fit
steps.instruction: Trim the pad so it sits snugly in the filter housing with no gaps at the edges.

steps.title: Rinse in tank water
steps.instruction: Rinse the new pad in a bucket of water taken from the tank before fitting it.

steps.title: Fit and check the flow
steps.instruction: Place the pad in the housing, restart the water flow and check that water passes through the pad rather than around it.

cautions: Clean a used pad in tank water, not tap water; chlorine in tap water can harm the helpful bacteria living on it.
Replace the pad when it tears or stays clogged after rinsing.

steps.title: Take the sample
steps.instruction: Fill the test tube from about an arm’s length below the surface, away from the inlet, at the same time of day each time you test.

steps.title: Add the drops in order
steps.instruction: Add the reagent drops in the order the kit's card gives and wait the time it says.

steps.title: Read in daylight
steps.instruction: Hold the tube against the white side of the colour card in daylight and pick the closest colour.

steps.title: Check your readings
steps.instruction: Enter the readings in the water safety check to compare them with the suggested ranges for your fish.

cautions: Keep the reagents away from children, and never pour them into the pond or tank.
Check the expiry date on each bottle; old reagents can give wrong colours.

waterProblemProducts.whyRelevant: An aerator adds oxygen to the water and may help while you look for the cause of the low reading.
A filter pad catches uneaten feed and waste before it breaks down into ammonia.
A test kit lets you recheck ammonia over the next few days to see whether it is coming down.
